findings.title: Architectural divergence between audit and remediate orchestrators violates 'One pipeline, two halves' core conviction
findings.summary:
The project's primary design conviction (enforced in CLAUDE.md, README.md, and docs/project-philosophy.md) is that auditing and remediating are not two separate tools, but 'two cases of ONE logical core, drawn read-only or write-and-apply.' However, the actual implementation exhibits structural fork divergence. src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts was introduced as a seed for shared obligation selection, but neither src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts nor src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts imports or uses it. Instead, src/audit uses an artifact DAG-based obligation priority scan over registered EXECUTOR_REGISTRY runner definitions, while src/remediate drives execution via a custom 5,500+ line imperative state machine with embedded stage functions (applyPlanPipeline, runTriagePhase, runClosePhase). Furthermore, provider wrappers (src/audit/providers/* vs src/remediate/providers/*) duplicate adapter wiring rather than expressing policy parameters over a single shared factory.

findings.description: Contract (tier-2, line 116-120 of findingIdentitySignature.ts): two fileless findings of the same lens+category always collapse to one identity (`rule|<lens>|<category>`). In the remediation state store, `items[finding_id]` keyed on the unstable `SEC-<hash8>-1` may bind to a different finding on the next `next-step` run (if synthesis order changes), causing the remediator to apply fix A to finding B.

findings.title: Node-worktree CWD guard relies on env var `AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD` that any worker process can forge, bypassing the shared-state-write protection
findings.description: Contract: the worktree guard detects when a CLI is invoked from a per-node worktree context and refuses shared-state writes; the mechanical discriminator is the CWD, not an easily-forgeable token. Trust boundary: the guard reads `process.env[AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD_ENV]` (line 96) as a candidate CWD, under the assumption that only the wrapper stamps it and that workers never inherit it (exec.ts:316 strips it from provider spawns). Counterexample: a worker agent, when instructed by a compromised or hallucinating host prompt, runs `AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD=/tmp/safe remediate-code next-step` from inside `.audit-tools/worktrees/remediate-block1-run1/`. `cwdCandidates` at line 94-97 returns ONLY `[explicitCwd]` when it is defined — but `explicitCwd` is a test-seam parameter, not the env var path. With no explicit override, both `fromEnv` (`/tmp/safe`, not a worktree) and `process.cwd()` (the worktree) are checked. BUT: if the worker sets `AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD` to any non-worktree path (e.g. `/`), `fromEnv` is non-null and added as the FIRST candidate; `nodeWorktreeAncestor('/')` returns null; `process.cwd()` IS the worktree but comes SECOND in the array. Since the guard throws on ANY candidate being in a worktree (line 121-126), both candidates are checked and the cwd probe fires. However, in the wrapper path the existing strip at exec.ts:316 removes the env var before spawning, so a worker that sets its own `AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD` overrides the stripped value. Given the var is consumed directly from `process.env` without signature verification, a malicious or misconfigured worker can supply any value.

findings.description: Contract: `setQuotaStateDir(dir)` is called ONCE at CLI entry and governs all subsequent quota reads/writes; `getQuotaStatePath()` throws if not called. findings.title: Stale-lock steal race: concurrent stealers can leave lockPath.steal orphaned without any holder writing the main lock, causing perpetual budget-free admission
findings.description: Contract: only ONE acquirer wins the `.steal` claim sidecar via exclusive `wx`; the single winner removes the stale lock; all others back off and retry the ordinary acquire path. Attack: process A wins the `.steal` claim and dies immediately after `writeFile(claimPath)` but BEFORE reading `lockPath`. The claim file now exists with A's token. Process B calls `stat(claimPath)` and sees `mtimeMs` <= STALE_LOCK_MS (A died milliseconds ago), so B does NOT reclaim the claim. B instead returns early from `stealStaleLock` (line 108: `return`). Process C arrives after STALE_LOCK_MS has elapsed; it stat's the claim as stale, unlinks it, then exits `stealStaleLock` with no lock removal either. The main lock file still carries the original stale token (never unlinked by anyone), and from now on every new stale check reads it as fresh because its mtime was never updated. In environments where `now()` drift or test-clock injection exceeds `STALE_LOCK_MS` the stale cycle re-fires, but a real crash window leaves the lock permanently wedged until the file's mtime on the filesystem naturally ages. Separately, `readStaleLockToken` performs a `stat` then a `readFile` non-atomically (lines 43–45): after the stat proves stale, the lock holder may refresh its heartbeat (touch the file), causing the mtime to advance so the token is read from a NOW-FRESH lock. `stealStaleLock` then passes `staleToken` as the previously-observed stale token, and at line 119 performs a token-equality read — but only if the file content STILL matches. If the heartbeat racing between stat and readFile results in a content change, the unlink is suppressed (correct), but the claim sidecar is already created and held. The claim stays alive until it self-expires (STALE_LOCK_MS), blocking all OTHER stealers from stealing a genuinely-stale successor lock that may arrive during that window.

findings.title: A third, unhardened copy of the cmd.exe shim-quoting logic lives in the build module
findings.summary: wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-build.mjs carries its own resolveSpawn with inline quoting that only doubles embedded quotes. findings.title: Asymmetric persistence models break DAG-based staleness propagation across remediation workflows
findings.summary:
The system's core continuity model asserts that 'Artifacts are continuity; dependency DAG is truth' and that staleness must propagate along an explicit dependency map without ad-hoc freshness checks. src/audit enforces this via src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts and src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts. However, src/remediate uses a dual persistence mechanism: a single monolithic RemediationState JSON document (src/remediate/state/store.ts) combined with scattered, ad-hoc disk existence checks for sidecar files (contractPipelineDir, nodeClaimsPath, intake sidecars).
Recommendation: Extend the shared dependency DAG model to cover remediation artifacts. Express contract pipeline stages and implementation outputs as nodes in the DAG so that upstream changes (such as updated intent or modified audit findings) automatically propagate staleness downstream rather than relying on imperative existsSync checks.

Whatever validation rules the tests assert are therefore the rules that happen to be compiled into dist/ at that moment, so running the suite without a preceding build (the documented single-test invocation `npx vitest run tests/audit/<file>.test.ts`) validates stale logic and reports green.
evidence: dispatch/validate.mjs:1 - the entire validation verdict comes from the compiled tree, never from src/.
dispatch/merge-results.mjs:4 - the schema-pointer exclusion set the merge relies on is likewise read from dist/.
tests/audit/dispatch-scripts.test.ts:17-22 - the tests spawn these scripts as child processes, so they inherit whatever dist/ contains and have no way to detect that it is stale.
package.json:48 - only `npm test` chains a build; the per-file vitest invocation documented for single tests does not, leaving a green-on-stale-build path open.

findings.title: Fragmented quota pool initialization and claim management between audit and remediation dispatch engines
findings.summary:
Both orchestrators dispatch LLM workloads using rolling engines and multi-worker pools, but quota allocation, rate-limit parsing, and pool claim management are duplicated between src/audit/cli/dispatch/quotaPool.ts and src/remediate/steps/dispatch.ts. While src/shared/quota/apiPool.ts defines shared quota structures, each orchestrator independently initializes capacity pools, parses host limits, and handles lease acquisition backoffs.
Recommendation: Consolidate quota pool initialization, lease claim backoffs, and sliding-window rate tracking into a single manager in src/shared/quota/. Both audit and remediate dispatchers should consume this unified manager to guarantee shared rate-limit awareness and prevent claim collisions or over-dispatch when both orchestrators execute concurrently.

findings.title: Space-delimited pair keys corrupt coupling edges for any path containing a space
findings.summary: Both coupling extractors encode a file pair as `${a} ${b}` and then decode it with key.indexOf(" "), which splits at the FIRST space rather than the delimiter. A cache written by an older shape (or hand-edited/partially written) is either consumed as a mis-typed object whose reuse decision reads undefined keys, or, if the file is malformed JSON, throws out of the bundle load instead of degrading to a cold rebuild.

affected_files.quoted_text:
* The cache is an internal incremental-reuse artifact, NOT a deliverable and NOT a
 * staleness-DAG node: it is self-describing (it carries the global `path_lookup_hash`
 * and a per-file `content_key`), so reuse validity is decided entirely by comparing
 * those against the fresh build — no `artifact_metadata` baseline is needed. Loaded
 * specially in `loadArtifactBundle` and written specially in `writeCoreArtifacts`
 * (the same pattern as `active_dispatch` / `design_review_snapshots`), so it never
 * needs an `ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS` entry or a dependency-map row.

evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/graphEdgeCache.ts:25 - readOptionalJsonFile<GraphEdgeCache> is a bare generic cast; there is no zod parse, no isRecord check and no field guard between disk and the caller.

src/audit/orchestrator/graphEdgeCache.ts:4-10 - the doc confirms the artifact is deliberately outside every registry that would otherwise validate or stale it, so this reader is the only trust boundary it has.

src/audit/orchestrator/graphEdgeCache.ts:16-33 - the persisted document carries no schema_version / contract_version, so an old-shape cache from a prior release is indistinguishable from a current one.
src/shared/io/json.ts:266-277 - readOptionalJsonFile rethrows anything that is not a file-missing error, so a truncated cache file is fatal to the load rather than a cache miss.

findings.title: The quota-escalation test polls up to 2s for a fire-and-forget friction write

findings.title: `acceptReconcile` trusts `git log --grep` substring match filtered to exact subject equality, but the filter compares using JavaScript `===` against a potentially multi-line stdout split; a trailing `\r` on Windows makes every commit invisible to the reconciler
findings.description:
Contract: `landedCommitsForBlock` returns the set of base-reachable commits whose subject EXACTLY equals the tool-owned subject (`remediate <blockId> (<runId>)`). Trust boundary: the filter at line 84 (`s === subject`) is the authoritative exact-match gate; a human commit mentioning the subject string but with a different subject never counts as landed evidence. Attack: on Windows, `git log --format=%H%x1f%s HEAD` emits lines terminated by `
`. `spawnSyncHidden` captures stdout as `encoding: 'utf8'`. `log.stdout.split('
')` at line 82 splits on `
` only; each resulting element retains a trailing ``. After `line.split('\x1f')`, `s` becomes `'remediate <blockId> (<runId>)'`. The strict equality `s === subject` (where `subject` has no trailing ``) fails. Every landing commit is invisible to the reconciler. Consequently, `reconcileAcceptOutcomes` never finds landed evidence, leaves all items in `in-progress` status, and the close phase treats every block as unreconciled. If the run was killed between `mergeWorktree` and `recordNodeAcceptOutcome` (window 1), the close phase marks the actually-landed block as `blocked` and omits its files from the staging manifest — the landed fix is silently dropped from the commit.

findings.title: `writeQuotaState` normalizes quota-state entries and silently drops any field not in the explicit allowlist; a future schema extension lands in memory but is erased on the next RMW cycle
findings.description: Contract: `writeQuotaState` performs schema migration: a v1 file read back round-trips safely. `normalizeEntry` projects onto the v2 field set (lines 200-212) by explicitly enumerating permitted fields: `updated_at`, `cooldown_until`, `last_429_at`, `consecutive_429_count`, `tokens_per_pct`, `output_per_input`. Counterexample: a future release adds a `warm_start_tokens` field to `QuotaStateEntry` and begins writing it in `recordOutputRatioObservation`. The first write persists the field. On the SECOND write cycle, `readQuotaStateForUpdate` reads the file back — the new field is in the parsed object — but `withFileLock` calls `writeQuotaState`, which calls `normalizeEntry`, which does NOT copy `warm_start_tokens` (it's not in the explicit allowlist). The field is silently erased. The quota state of a long-running run gradually loses learned data that was added in a newer build. The invariant-comment on `normalizeEntry` at line 193 explicitly says "Writing is the migration" — but the migration is one-way destructive, not additive. Any field added to `QuotaStateEntry` in the TypeScript type that is not also added to `normalizeEntry` is silently dropped on first write.

findings.title: Cherry-pick in `mergeWorktree` is not guarded by a pre-flight dirty-file check for ALL tracked files, only files touched by the branch; a pre-existing dirty tracked file outside the branch's edit set silently passes then fails git cherry-pick
findings.description: Contract: `dirtyMainTreeCollisions` detects pre-existing dirty tracked files that would block the cherry-pick and surfaces an actionable error. Implementation: the function (lines 326-346) calls `gitEditedFilesForBranch(root, branch)` to get files the branch edits, then runs `git status --porcelain -- <those files>`. Counterexample: the branch edits only `src/foo.ts`. The main checkout has `src/bar.ts` dirty (unrelated WIP). `git cherry-pick <tip>` applied to a commit that only touches `src/foo.ts` will succeed even if `src/bar.ts` is dirty, because git only conflicts on files the commit TOUCHES. The collision guard correctly doesn't report `src/bar.ts` — that is fine for this scenario. HOWEVER: if the branch edit set is empty (no committed files — e.g. the worktree only made untracked changes that `commitWorktree` added with `git add --force`), `gitEditedFilesForBranch` may return `available: true` with an empty `files` set. `dirtyMainTreeCollisions` then returns `[]` (line 328: `edited.files.size === 0`). The cherry-pick proceeds against a commit that IS non-empty (it committed untracked files), but no collision check ran. A dirty file that git would have flagged is silently missed. Additionally, `mergeWorktree` at line 279-311 does NOT call `dirtyMainTreeCollisions` itself — that call lives in `acceptNodeWorktree` in acceptNode.ts, which passes `dirtyMainTreeCollisions(root, branch)` upstream. Any caller of `mergeWorktree` that does not call `dirtyMainTreeCollisions` first skips the guard entirely.

findings.title: Child stdin has no `error` listener; an EPIPE while piping the prompt raises an unhandled stream error

findings.title: Content-key `redispatch` discriminator requires `attempt` as a non-optional input but `resultDiscriminatorForEmit` passes `opts.attempt!` (non-null assertion) without a runtime guard — a missing attempt silently produces `NaN` in the key

If the caller passes `source='redispatch'` with `opts.attempt` undefined (e.g. through a dynamic spread object where `attempt` was unset), TypeScript compiles successfully (the `!` suppresses the type error), and `opts.attempt!` evaluates to `undefined` at runtime. `baseDiscriminator` at line 245-265 then constructs the discriminator string as `source:${input.attempt}` = `'redispatch:undefined'`. This string is fed into the idempotency key hash. Two distinct re-dispatch attempts (attempt 1 and attempt 2) should produce distinct keys; both produce `redispatch:undefined` and collapse to the SAME idempotencyKey. The second attempt's result is treated as a duplicate of the first (INV-2 gate) and silently dropped — a re-dispatch that genuinely fixed the output never gets ingested.

findings.title: Contract-pipeline semantic-projection hash strips only two field names ('created_at','generated_at'); a new non-semantic field bypasses the strip and phantom-stales the entire downstream chain
findings.description: Contract (B3): staleness is keyed on semantic projections, not raw bytes, so a cosmetic edit to a field the downstream does not consume does NOT re-stale downstreams. The UNIVERSAL_NON_SEMANTIC_FIELDS allowlist (line 38) is `["created_at","generated_at"]`. Counterexample: a future host-authored artifact gains a `run_id` provenance field (plausible — audit-code's `access_memory.json` already uses `run_id`, stripped via `NON_SEMANTIC_FIELDS_BY_ARTIFACT` in artifactFreshness.ts). That field is NOT in `UNIVERSAL_NON_SEMANTIC_FIELDS`, so every re-generation of the artifact emits a new `run_id`, changing `semanticProjection` output, changing `payloadSemanticHash`, and marking every downstream artifact stale. The result is finalization oscillation: obligation_ledger → test_validator_plan → contract_assessment_report → counterexample → judge_report → implementation_dag all re-fire on each step even though no load-bearing content changed. The DEPENDENCY_MAP at artifactStore.ts:58-91 shows that `counterexample` depends on 6 upstreams — a single phantom-stale `goal_spec` re-stales all six levels. The problem is amplified because `envelopeSemanticHash` (line 207-210) is computed from the STORED envelope's payload, meaning a tool-stamped field added after initial write causes all future reads to see a changed hash against a never-changing stored `dependency_hashes`, making every re-open of a pipeline stale.

findings.title: Full-frontier rolling drive silently skips planned blocks that form no dependency level, then the merge terminal-blocks them
findings.summary: driveRollingImplementDispatch plans a block set with prepareImplementDispatch (dependency-eligibility only) but drives `rollingDependencyLevels`, which additionally applies the phase barrier and drops permanently-ineligible nodes; the resulting empty-or-narrower level set is guarded only for a partition-scoped caller, so on the full-frontier path a planned-but-unlevelled block is never dispatched and then blocked by mergeImplementResults for a result file it was never allowed to produce.
evidence: src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:1327-1330 - the code itself names this hazard for the partition case: "a partition caller following that recipe against the just-written full-frontier plan would terminal-block every undriven block (review h2c2 F1)". The identical hazard on the full-frontier path has no guard.
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2378-2383 - prepareImplementDispatch "only admits verified-complete-eligible blocks (dependencyVerifiedComplete)"; that predicate does not consider `phase_ordinal`.

src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:644-664 - rollingDependencyLevels adds the phase barrier (phaseBarrierClear / phaseBarrierUnsatisfiable) on top of the dependency edges, so it can exclude a block the plan admitted.

src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:1533 - after the drive, `mergeImplementResults` runs unconditionally over the whole plan on the full-frontier path, so an undriven planned block is reconciled as missing.

findings.failure_scenario: Plan has block Z (phase 0, already `blocked`), block A (phase 0, pending, depends on Z) and block B (phase 1, pending, no dependencies). prepareImplementDispatch admits B (its dependency set is empty, so dependencyVerifiedComplete holds) but not A (Z is not verified-complete). rollingDependencyLevels marks A permanently ineligible (dep Z blocked) and B permanently ineligible (phaseBarrierUnsatisfiable(1) — Z at a lower phase is neither verified nor pending), so `levels` is empty. `partitionIds` is null, so the empty-partition guard at 1331 does not apply; driveRollingDispatch dispatches nothing and mergeImplementResults at 1533 then blocks B for a missing result file even though the tool itself wrote B's prompt and result path and never ran it.

findings.title: Gate commands are gated on directory structure alone, so a missing or renamed npm script becomes a rollback-triggering false red instead of a scope-out
findings.summary: `isAuditToolsMonorepo` probes five filesystem paths and never checks that the npm scripts the derived commands invoke exist. `mergedGuardSuiteArgv` then returns `npm run verify:guards` (and `mergedBaseCheckArgv` returns `npm run check`) for any tree with that shape. findings.title: gate/test jobs in publish-package.yml run with no explicit least-privilege permissions
findings.summary: publish-package.yml has no top-level `permissions:` block, and the `gate` and `test` jobs (which check out the repo and run arbitrary npm install/build/test scripts) declare no job-level `permissions:` either, so they run with the repository/org default GITHUB_TOKEN scope instead of an explicit least-privilege grant — unlike ci.yml, which sets `permissions: contents: read` top-level, and unlike the `publish` job in this same file, which explicitly scopes itself to `contents: read` / `id-token: write`.
evidence: .github/workflows/publish-package.yml:46 - the `gate` job (and likewise `test` at line 74) has no `permissions:` key, so it inherits the repo/org default GITHUB_TOKEN scope rather than an explicit least-privilege grant.
.github/workflows/publish-package.yml:126 - only the `publish` job explicitly scopes permissions, showing the pattern is known and used in this exact file but not applied to `gate`/`test`.
.github/workflows/ci.yml:59 - ci.yml sets an explicit top-level `permissions: contents: read`, the same restriction publish-package.yml omits for its own checkout+build+test jobs.

findings.title: globMatches translates '**/' so it always requires a directory separator, so a leading-globstar pattern never matches a repo-root file
findings.summary: The glob-to-regex translation maps '**' to '.*' and then emits the following '/' literally, so a pattern such as '**/*.env' compiles to ^.*/[^/]*\.env$ and cannot match a root-level path like '.env'. Under standard globstar semantics '**/' matches zero or more directories, so a must_not_touch entry written that way silently fails to exclude root-level files from both orchestrators' scope.
evidence: src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:41 - '**' consumes both stars and emits '.*', leaving the pattern's following '/' to be appended as a mandatory literal separator
src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:54 - the resulting regex is anchored with ^ and $, so the mandatory '/' cannot be skipped for a path with no directory component

src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:95 - must_not_touch entries (bare globs by contract) are matched exclusively through globMatches, so a write-forbidden root-level file is reported as in scope by both orchestrators

src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:9 - the module is documented as the single authority whose per-file exclusion must be identical on both sides, which makes a silent under-match a scope-policy defect rather than a cosmetic one

findings.title: lineIndex silently last-wins on conflicting per-file line counts across sibling tasks, feeding a hard-reject gate
findings.summary: The expected-line-count index is built by flattening every packet task's file_line_counts into one object, so when two sibling tasks in the same packet declare different counts for the same path, the later entry silently overwrites the earlier one. findings.title: Reservation ledger `admit` uses `Date.now()` directly for the lease `expiresAt` while the `ReservationLedger.now` injectable clock is only used in `sumOutstanding` and `pruneExpired`; test clocks cannot control lease expiry
findings.description: Contract (INV-QD-15 / doc comment): every time read inside the lock routes through the injectable `now` clock so a single injected clock governs the whole admission. `mintLeaseId` (line 151-153) uses `Date.now()` directly, not `this.now()`. More critically: in `admit` (line 352-353), the `expiresAt` is `now + ttl` where `now = this.now()` — this part IS correct. BUT `mintLeaseId` also calls `Date.now()` for the token portion, which is fine since it is opaque. HOWEVER: `reconcile` and `outstanding` both call `withFileLock(this.lockPath, ...)` and inside call `const now = this.now()`, then `pruneExpired(..., now)` — these ARE injectable. The critical gap is `reclaimExpired` at line 403-409: it also uses `this.now()` correctly. So the clock injection IS mostly consistent. The real contract break: `STALE_LOCK_MS` (the default lease TTL at line 284) is the file-lock staleness window (30s), which is far shorter than `DISPATCH_LEASE_TTL_MS` (20 min, line 48). A caller that constructs `new ReservationLedger(path)` without the explicit `DISPATCH_LEASE_TTL_MS` default gets leases that expire in 30 seconds — far too short for real LLM dispatches. The export `createReservationLedger()` at line 446 uses the no-args constructor, inheriting the 30s default. Dispatch code using `createReservationLedger()` without passing `DISPATCH_LEASE_TTL_MS` at admit time will have leases expire mid-flight, silently releasing budget that is still actively in use and enabling double-grants.

findings.title: Staleness propagation skips transitive re-firing across slice-projected edges, creating a window where a deeply-stale upstream leaves a downstream artifact fresh until an explicit drain
findings.description: Contract: the slice-protected edge optimization (lines 207-223) blocks TRANSITIVE staleness propagation across an edge that has a registered slice projection AND a recorded slice. Rationale: the downstream's staleness is decided by the per-edge slice compare AFTER the upstream re-derives, not pre-emptively. Attack: artifact A → B → C, where B→C has a slice projection. A becomes stale (e.g. due to an upstream change outside B's slice). The propagation loop at lines 195-228 marks B stale (A is its direct upstream with no slice). When propagating from B to C, lines 217-222 check `entry?.dependency_slices?.[upstream]` for C's record of B. If C was written with a recorded slice (from a prior run), the check succeeds and BLOCKS C's transitive marking. C stays fresh. Now B re-derives and emits IDENTICAL slice content (the upstream A change was outside B's slice-projected fields). C's stored slice matches the re-derived B slice — correct outcome. BUT: if B's re-derivation DOES change the slice (A's change was in B's consumed fields), C should be stale. The drain loop re-derives B in step N, emitting a new slice. At step N+1, `computeStaleArtifacts` re-runs and NOW marks C stale via per-edge slice compare. However, the doc comment says "the downstream's staleness re-derives each drain iteration" — this assumes the drain continues. If `advanceAudit` returns early (MAX_DRAIN_STEPS=64 hit), the re-derived B is persisted but C is still fresh. C then dispatches to an LLM with stale slice-relative content from a prior B, producing incorrect results without any staleness signal.

findings.title: The `run_start_dirty` snapshot is never re-captured on a re-plan; files dirtied by a first partial run and then abandoned are incorrectly excluded from the staging manifest on the re-plan's close
findings.description: Contract: `run_start_dirty` is captured once at the extracted-plan join site and NEVER re-captured on a re-plan, because re-capturing after edits landed would wrongly classify the run's own hand-applied work as pre-existing dirt. `resolveEditSurfaceManifest` at close.ts:521 uses `run_start_dirty` to exclude declared files from the staging manifest — the assumption is that any file in `run_start_dirty` predates the run. Counterexample: a user starts a remediation run, which partially edits `src/auth.ts` (dirtying it). The user then re-plans (e.g. via a triage halt-and-restart). At the re-plan join site (nextStep.ts:2748), `run_start_dirty` is preserved from the prior `existing` state (nextStep.ts:1801: `...(previous.run_start_dirty ? { run_start_dirty: previous.run_start_dirty } : {})`). The prior run's half-edited `src/auth.ts` is NOT in the original `run_start_dirty` (it was clean when the first run started). After re-plan, a new block declares `src/auth.ts` in its write scope. The re-plan's block resolves (fixing auth.ts). `resolveEditSurfaceManifest` at close finds `src/auth.ts` in `item.item_spec.touched_files`, does NOT find it in `run_start_dirty`, and includes it in the staging manifest. This is CORRECT for the re-plan. BUT: if instead the first run's partial edit to `src/auth.ts` was committed to `applied_edit_surface` (source 1), and the re-plan's block also lists `src/auth.ts` in touched_files (source 2), the path appears twice in the union — still correct (de-duped by `Set`). The real failure is the REVERSE: if the user MANUALLY reverts `src/auth.ts` (making it clean again) after the first run partially fails, then the re-plan's `run_start_dirty` does NOT contain `src/auth.ts` (because it was clean at first-run start and is clean now). But if the re-plan block touches it, the staging manifest correctly includes it. The actual breakage: if `run_start_dirty` from a PRIOR run of a different session is somehow re-loaded through state.json persistence, files dirty in session A are excluded from session B's staging manifest even though session B started with them clean.

findings.title: The quota-state file-lock `LOCKED_JSON_STORE_TIMEOUT_MS` is derived as `STALE_LOCK_MS - 10_000 = 20s`, but a heartbeat that fires every 10s (HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS = STALE_LOCK_MS/3 ≈ 10s) can miss two beats within the 30s stale window, allowing a LIVE lock to be stolen while the holder still has 0–10s remaining on its timeout
findings.description: Contract: the heartbeat fires at STALE_LOCK_MS/3 intervals so that even two missed beats leave the lock fresh (doc comment line 143). STALE_LOCK_MS=30,000ms; HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS=10,000ms. With two missed beats the lock's mtime is last-updated at T=10s. At T=30s it becomes stale. The lock is HELD for up to LOCKED_JSON_STORE_TIMEOUT_MS=20,000ms. But the critical section INSIDE `withFileLock` can legitimately run for almost 20s before the lock is released. Timeline: lock acquired at T=0. First heartbeat fires at T=10s (ok). Second heartbeat should fire at T=20s. Node event loop stall (GC pause, slow FS) delays it by 11s. At T=31s the mtime is still T=10s (beat 1). `readStaleLockToken` fires at a stale-checking peer: `now() - info.mtimeMs = 21s > 30s`? No — 31-10=21 < 30s. Still fresh. GC stall ends. Third heartbeat fires at T=31s. A new stale-check peer at T=40s: `40 - 31 = 9 < 30s`. Still fine. More adversarially: two consecutive GC pauses of 11s each. Beat 1 at T=10. Beat 2 delayed to T=33 (11s overrun of 22s interval). At T=33+10 = T=43 another peer checks: `43 - 10 = 33 > 30` → STALE. Lock is stolen. The holder is STILL inside its 20s lock timeout window (acquired at T=0, now at T=43 = 43s in, which is PAST the 20s timeout — so the acquire would have timed out at T=20 anyway). The scenario actually demonstrates that the TIMEOUT is the binding constraint, not the heartbeat math. HOWEVER: the comment at line 143 says 'even two consecutive missed beats ... leave the lock fresh' — this is only true if the interval timer fires exactly on schedule. Under high CPU/GC load, Node's `setInterval` jitter can exceed 100ms per tick, and two beats each delayed by HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS/2 result in the lock looking stale before the critical section completes. The doc comment's guarantee is non-deterministic under load.

findings.title: Transient read failures are reported as 'Invalid JSON' and classified terminal, so an EBUSY/EACCES blip permanently fails the task
findings.summary: Any non-ENOENT error from `readFile` — EACCES, EBUSY/EPERM (routine on Windows), EMFILE, or a read that catches a worker mid-write — is funneled into `kind: "unparseable"` with the message 'Invalid JSON'. That kind never defers by design, so a transient IO failure is treated as an arrived-and-invalid result: the claim is cleared, the task is written to failed-tasks.json, and the merge exits 2.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:366-367 - the deferral policy relies on 'unparseable' meaning a result genuinely arrived, an assumption a failed read violates.

There is no re-read or backoff on the result file, so a worker writing its result non-atomically can be observed truncated exactly once and be recorded as a contract failure.

findings.title: Windows shim wrapping is limited to four hardcoded package-manager names, so every other .cmd/.bat shim spawns raw

findings.title: brokered-dispatch-no-disk-io.test.ts's banned-symbol and floating-promise checks have reach holes and false-RED surface
findings.summary: The comment stripper only removes FULL-LINE `//` comments, so a trailing `// getQuotaStatePath` note on a code line false-REDs the banned-symbol check; conversely the banned check is a plain substring test that also fires on any string literal containing the name. findings.title: climbOutOfAuditTools matches the .audit-tools segment case-sensitively while the sibling worktree guard is deliberately case-insensitive
findings.summary: `climbOutOfAuditTools` locates the artifact-tree segment with a case-sensitive `Array.prototype.indexOf`, whereas `nodeWorktreeAncestor` lowercases each segment specifically because win32 paths are case-insensitive. On win32 a cwd re-cased as `.AUDIT-TOOLS` therefore fires the worktree refusal but is NOT climbed out of by the repo-root resolver, so the drift pathology the resolver exists to prevent (a phantom nested artifact tree) is reachable again.
evidence: src/shared/io/repoRoot.ts:36 - `segments.indexOf(AUDIT_TOOLS_DIRNAME)` is an exact, case-sensitive comparison.
src/shared/io/nodeWorktreeGuard.ts:46-50 - the comment states the rationale explicitly: 'win32 paths are case-preserving but case-insensitive, so a re-cased cwd must still be detected'.

src/shared/io/nodeWorktreeGuard.ts:39-42 - `nodeWorktreeAncestor`'s doc claims it matches the outermost segment run 'consistent with `climbOutOfAuditTools`', but the two use different comparison semantics on the same directory name.

findings.title: Entrypoint-flow bridge edges are last-write-wins, so a longer path's confidence overwrites the shortest path's
findings.summary: `buildEntrypointFlowBridgeEdges` keys discovered bridges on `from\0to\0kind` and stores each with `Map.set`, so when two distinct paths from the same root reach the same target the later (longer, and by construction min-confidence-over-more-hops) discovery replaces the earlier one. The emitted edge's `confidence` and `reason` then describe the last path found rather than the strongest/shortest.
evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketGraphClustering.ts:596 - `bridgeEdges` is a plain Map; the write at line 651 is an unconditional `set`, with no compare against an already-recorded confidence.

src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketGraphClustering.ts:639 - confidence is the min over the traversed edges, so a longer path is monotonically weaker; overwriting it with the later discovery records the weaker value.
src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketGraphClustering.ts:606-609 - the queue is FIFO (level-order), so the FIRST discovery is the fewest-hop path — the one that should win.
src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketGraphEdges.ts:71-83 - `isPacketExpansionEdge` gates merges on confidence, so an under-recorded bridge confidence can flip a packet merge decision.

findings.title: Fan-out pause counter starts at 0, so the livelock bound fires one walled pass late
findings.summary: advanceFanoutPause persists pause_count: 0 on the FIRST wall and returns without ever consulting checkLivelockGuard, so the count it later passes excludes the first pause — but checkLivelockGuard documents its pauseCount parameter as 'inclusive of the current one'. A permanently-walled fan-out family therefore burns LIVELOCK_PAUSE_LIMIT + 1 walled next-step passes before the enrichment is skipped, not LIVELOCK_PAUSE_LIMIT.
evidence: src/audit/cli/dispatch/hostFanoutGate.ts:119-126 - the first wall (no prior file) writes pause_count: 0 and returns false; the guard is never called on that pass, so the first pause is not counted.

src/audit/cli/dispatch/hostFanoutGate.ts:127-130 - the second wall computes nextCount = prior.pause_count + 1 = 1 and only then calls checkLivelockGuard(nextCount, 0, livelockLimit); after k walls the persisted count is k-1.
src/shared/rolling/pausedState.ts:101 - the parameter contract states pauseCount is the 'Number of consecutive pauses recorded so far (inclusive of the current one)', which the fan-out path violates.
src/shared/rolling/pausedState.ts:67 - LIVELOCK_PAUSE_LIMIT = 3, so the skip lands on the 4th walled pass instead of the 3rd.

findings.title: git-history paths are scope-filtered case-insensitively but consumed with exact-match lookups
findings.summary: mineGitHistoryArtifact keeps a mined path when its NORMALIZED, lowercased key is in scope, but the retained entries carry git's raw spelling. themes.title: Architectural Divergence & Remediation Monoliths (Design Critique)
themes.root_cause: Structural drift away from the core 'one pipeline, two halves' philosophy, resulting in duplicated provider/orchestrator abstractions and a monolithic, imperative 5,500+ line remediation state machine.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Unify audit and remediate orchestrators onto a single shared ObligationEngine and refactor monolithic state machines into modular, declarative executor pipelines.

themes.title: Test Suite Masking, Tautological Verification & Drift (Test Quality Assessment)
themes.root_cause: Test suites swallow environment failures (e.g. git init failures leading to early returns), execute tautological assertions (expect(true).toBeTruthy()), test hand-copied local code duplicates, or scan non-existent package directories.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Fail test setup loudly on fixture creation errors, replace local re-implementations and tautology assertions with actual module imports, and fix invariant path patterns.

themes.title: Flawed Graph Algorithms, Scope Canonicalization & Contract Handlers (Contract Assessment)
themes.root_cause: Algorithmic defects in dependency-cycle topological tiering, uncanonicalized path matching in ownership claims, unhandled JSON parsing exceptions in worker state merges, and broken factory argument forwarding.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Correct cycle memoization and topological ordering logic, enforce physical file path canonicalization, wrap worker parsing in fault-tolerant isolation handlers, and forward options correctly.

themes.title: Fail-Open Reliability Hazards, Non-Atomic Locks & Unbounded Executions
themes.root_cause: Verification gates fail open on git probe errors, suite locks write non-atomically and get wiped by concurrent readers, and process execution lacks timeouts, causing permanent process stalls.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Enforce fail-closed semantics on missing git evidence, introduce mandatory subprocess execution timeouts, and adopt temp-then-rename atomic writes for lock files.

themes.title: Unvalidated Intake Artifacts & Vacuous Verification Evidence Fabrication
themes.root_cause: JSON artifacts are cast without runtime schema validation, file read errors are recorded as zero line counts that auto-exclude source files, and verification outcomes record pass status when tests never ran.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Add strict runtime JSON schema validation, use explicit null/undefined sentinels for unreadable line counts, and report un-executed test suites as unverified or skipped.

themes.title: Un-allowlisted Task Command Execution & Permissive Credential Permissions
themes.root_cause: Task validation spawns arbitrary commands from persisted JSON artifacts without allowlist checking, and credential rotation writes OAuth tokens with default permissive file modes.
themes.suggested_fix_pattern: Enforce strict command allowlist validation for task execution and explicitly set 0600 permissions when writing OAuth credential files.

executive_summary: The deterministic code audit of the audit-tools repository identified 2,100 total findings, including 121 high-severity issues spanning system architecture, test suite integrity, contract pipeline algorithms, reliability, data integrity, and security. Critical risks stem from structural divergence between audit and remediation orchestrators, widespread false-green test suites masking missing git setup or asserting tautologies, and contract pipeline phase-cut algorithms that dispatch cyclic modules before their dependencies. Furthermore, verification gates fail open on git probe failures, unvalidated verification reports record fabricated test passes, and runtime task executors spawn un-allowlisted commands without execution timeouts.
top_risks: Design Critique: Architectural divergence between audit and remediate orchestrators violates the core 'one pipeline, two halves' principle, producing duplicated abstractions and a monolithic, high-complexity 5,500+ line remediation state machine.

Test Quality & False Assurance: Over 50 test files return early without assertions when git setup fails, assert tautologies like expect(true).toBeTruthy(), or test local code duplicates, providing illusory test coverage.
Algorithmic Dependency Ordering Failure: Cycle-resolution and phase-cut algorithms memoize invalid topological tiers, causing cyclic modules to be scheduled before their foundational dependencies.

Fail-Open Verification & Cherry-Pick Risk: Verification gates treat git probe errors as empty command sets, silently skipping per-node verification before cherry-picking unverified branches into main.
Vacuous Verification Evidence: Close-phase reports record 'combined test suite passed' and status 'passed' even when no test command was configured or executed, producing false compliance artifacts.
Unbounded Subprocesses & Execution Deadlocks: Subprocess spawns across close phases and validation steps lack timeouts and kill deadlines, allowing hung commands to lock the engine indefinitely.
